title: A Radical and Evidence-Based Rethinking of EdTech in Schools
author: Sophie Winkleman
summary: Sophie Winkleman's speech at the Alliance for Responsible Citizenship conference (introduced by Jon Haidt) makes an evidence-based case for removing internet-enabled devices from classrooms. She opens with a headteacher who canceled lessons and told children to go play—and they stood around awkwardly, unable to create their own entertainment. EdTech apps use the same slot-machine tactics (streaks, notifications, unpredictable rewards) that make social media harmful—not because they improve learning but because engagement is the business model. A 3,000-student PISA experiment found the paper-based group scored 20 points higher than the computer-based group (equivalent to six months of extra schooling). Neuroscience shows handwriting activates the whole brain while typing leaves it dark. AI in schools represents an intensified version of the same problem: immediate relief in exchange for long-term dependency, a trade-off that skips the 'crawling phase' of cognitive development children cannot recover.
points: Children given unstructured outdoor time in a school that had relied on screen-based learning couldn't create their own entertainment—they stood around awkwardly until they asked to come back inside.

EdTech apps embed the same design features regulators deem harmful in social media—streaks, daily rewards, unpredictable notifications—not because those features improve learning but because they improve engagement.
A 3,000-student PISA experiment found the paper-based group scored 20 points higher than the computer group—the equivalent of six months' extra schooling.

Neuroscience shows the whole brain lights up during handwriting while typing leaves it comparatively dark; handwriting's slower pace also forces students to organize and prioritize what they're recording.
AI in schools offers immediate elevation of results twinned with long-term dwindling of capability—the same dependency trade-off, but applied to the developmental window children cannot get back.
quotes: Boredom costs nothing and is a crucial catalyst for the imagination.
These features do not appear in educational products because they improve learning. They appear because they improve engagement, and engagement is what the business model requires.
Material read from a page in a book implants in the brain more profoundly than the exact same material read from a screen.
The paper-based group scored twenty points higher — the equivalent of six months’ extra schooling.
Immediate relief in exchange for long-term dependency seems to be AI’s defining trade-off: an instant elevation of results, twinned with a long-term dwindling of capability.
Orwell feared those who would ban books. Huxley feared there would be no reason to ban a book, for there would be no one left who wanted to read one.
